nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; Igbo novelist, short-story writer and children's author, born and raised in Northern Nigeria, who chaired Biafra's Bureau for External Publicity during the civil war
literary_identity: Nigerian novelist and pioneer of the popular urban novel, whose People of the City (1954) was among the first West African novels in English and whose Jagua Nana (1961) became the best-known Nigerian popular novel; also a prolific writer of folk tales, novellas and books for young readers from 1947 to the 1990s.
biography: Cyprian Odiatu Duaka Ekwensi was born on 26 September 1921 at Minna in Northern Nigeria, to Igbo parents from Nkwelle Ezunaka, in present-day Anambra State (Wikipedia). Contemporary Black Biography says that he grew up speaking Hausa as well as Igbo, and that his father, David Duaka, a storyteller and elephant hunter, told him the Igbo tales he later published. He was educated at Government College, Ibadan, at Achimota College in the Gold Coast and at the School of Forestry, worked for two years as a forestry officer, and taught biology, chemistry and English at Igbobi College, Lagos, from 1947 to 1949, the years of his first books. Trained as a pharmacist, he lectured at the School of Pharmacy in Lagos (1949-1956), and in 1951 a government scholarship took him to the Chelsea School of Pharmacy in London; he wrote People of the City on the voyage. Gale dates his first work for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation to 1951; Contemporary Authors makes him head of features there from 1957 to 1961, when he became federal director of information. He read his stories on the radio, where he was known as 'Your Favourite Story Teller'. In 1966 he resigned and moved his family to Enugu; during the civil war he chaired Biafra's Bureau for External Publicity and directed its radio service, and travelled to the United States to raise money for Biafra. After the war he ran newspaper and publishing companies in the East (managing director of the Daily Star, 1975-1979), chaired the East Central State Library Board (1972-1975) and, according to Gale, the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria from 1991; Contemporary Black Biography says he wrote full time from 1984. He received the Dag Hammarskjold International Prize for Literary Merit (1969 in Gale's entries, 1968 in Wikipedia), was made a Member of the Order of the Federal Republic in 2001 and a fellow of the Nigerian Academy of Letters in 2006, and died at Enugu on 4 November 2007. He married Eunice Anyiwo; they had five children.
literary_profile: Ekwensi's books of the period run from When Love Whispers and Ikolo the Wrestler (both 1947) to King Forever! and Masquerade Time (1992) and The Red Flag (1993). His adult novels are People of the City (1954), Jagua Nana (1961), Burning Grass (1962), Beautiful Feathers (1963), Iska (1966), Survive the Peace (1976), Divided We Stand (1980), and Jagua Nana's Daughter and For a Roll of Parchment (both 1986 or 1987). His collections of stories include The Rainmaker (1965), Lokotown (1966) and Restless City and Christmas Gold (1975), and Contemporary Authors lists twenty-one juvenile titles, among them The Leopard's Claw (1950), The Drummer Boy and The Passport of Mallam Ilia (1960) and An African Night's Entertainment (1962). He also wrote hundreds of stories for newspapers, magazines and radio, and radio and television scripts for the BBC and Radio Nigeria. Emmanuel Iduma puts his output at nearly forty novels by his death; Cosentino notes that the U.S. edition of Jagua Nana (1969) already listed seven novellas, four works of folklore, two collections of stories and six novels.
stylistic_characteristics: Ekwensi called himself 'a writer for the masses', more interested in 'the heart of the truth which the man in the street can recognize' than in style (interview with Lewis Nkosi, 1972, quoted in Contemporary Black Biography). His novels are episodic, a habit the Encyclopedia of World Biography traces to his beginnings as a pamphleteer and Contemporary Black Biography to the radio stories out of which People of the City grew. Juliet Okonkwo compares his naturalistic technique with Zola's; John Povey sees behind it a reading of American popular fiction and crime paperbacks. Dialogue moves between Pidgin, broken English and standard Nigerian English, sometimes within one paragraph, and his descriptions of dress borrow the language of advertising in Drum magazine (Cosentino).
intellectual_concerns: The modern West African city, above all Lagos, as a place of opportunity, corruption and moral danger for migrants from the countryside; women's independence and its price (Jagua Nana, Iska, Jagua Nana's Daughter); party politics and corruption at the end of colonial rule and after independence; Pan-African solidarity set against domestic failure (Beautiful Feathers); ethnic hostility, civil war and the hardships of the peace (Iska, Survive the Peace, Divided We Stand); colour prejudice met by African students in England (For a Roll of Parchment); and, in the folk tales and children's books, vengeance, heroism, adventure and moral instruction.
historical_significance: Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia calls him the father of the modern Nigerian novel, and Martin Tucker the earliest and most prolific of the socially realistic Nigerian novelists (quoted in Contemporary Authors). People of the City preceded Achebe's Things Fall Apart by four years, and Charles Larson thought him probably the most widely read novelist in Nigeria. His standing with critics has been lower: Bernth Lindfors found none of his works free of 'amateurish blots and blunders', while his biographer Ernest Emenyonu saw in them 'a literature of social awareness and commitment'. He links the Onitsha market pamphlets, where he began, with the novel published in London, and the St. James Guide to Children's Writers calls him an acknowledged pioneer of Nigerian writing for young readers.

After 2000: Cash on Delivery (stories, 2007, according to Wikipedia). Dates that differ between sources are given in the work records.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English, from a Tamil family of Madras, who lived in Mysore and set almost all his fiction in the imaginary South Indian town of Malgudi
literary_identity: Indian novelist and short-story writer, with Mulk Raj Anand and Raja Rao a leading author of early Indian writing in English (Wikipedia); his fourteen novels, from Swami and Friends (1935) to The World of Nagaraj (1990), are almost all set in Malgudi, as are most of his stories, and The Guide (1958) won the first Sahitya Akademi Award for a book in English.
biography: Rasipuram Krishnaswami Narayanaswami was born in Madras on 10 October 1906 into a Tamil Brahmin family and spent part of his childhood in the care of his maternal grandmother, Parvati, while his father, a headmaster, was transferred from school to school (Wikipedia). In 1922 he joined the school in Mysore where his father was headmaster; he failed the entrance examination twice and took his BA at Maharaja's College, Mysore, in 1930 (Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia; Contemporary Authors). A brief spell as a schoolteacher proved distasteful, and he turned to writing: an article on Indian cinema in the Madras Mail (July 1930) was his first publication, and he later reported from Mysore for the newspaper Justice. Graham Greene, shown the manuscript by a friend, recommended Swami and Friends, which Hamish Hamilton published in 1935; Contemporary Authors says he shortened his surname to Narayan that year. He married Rajam in 1934; they had a daughter, Hema, and Rajam's death in 1939 stopped his writing for a time. He edited the journal Indian Thought from 1941 and owned Indian Thought Publications in Mysore, which issued many of his books in India. After The English Teacher (1945) came the novels of the period studied here, from Mr. Sampath (1949) to The World of Nagaraj (1990), together with stories, essays, travel writing, a memoir and prose versions of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata; My Dateless Diary records his first visit to the United States, in 1956. His honours include the Sahitya Akademi Award for The Guide (1960; Contemporary Authors gives 1961), the Padma Bhushan (1964), the English-Speaking Union Book Award for My Days (1975), the Royal Society of Literature's Benson Medal (1980), honorary membership of the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters (1981 in Wikipedia, 1982 in Contemporary Authors), the Sahitya Akademi Fellowship (1994) and the Padma Vibhushan (2000). He sat in the Rajya Sabha as a nominated member from 1986 to 1992. His brother R. K. Laxman, the cartoonist, illustrated some of his books. He died in Chennai on 13 May 2001; his manuscripts are in the Mugar Memorial Library at Boston University.
literary_profile: Narayan's books of 1946-2000 comprise ten novels, from Mr. Sampath (1949) to The World of Nagaraj (1990); story collections from An Astrologer's Day and Other Stories (1947) and Lawley Road (1956) to Malgudi Days (1982), Under the Banyan Tree (1985), The Grandmother's Tale (1992) and Salt and Sawdust (1993); retellings of Indian myth in Gods, Demons, and Others (1964) and shortened prose versions of the Ramayana (1972) and the Mahabharata (1978); travel writing (My Dateless Diary, 1960; The Emerald Route, 1977, which includes the play The Watchman of the Lake); essays (Next Sunday, 1956; Reluctant Guru, 1974; A Writer's Nightmare, 1988); and the memoir My Days (1974). He also wrote stories for magazines, among them the New Yorker (Contemporary Authors) and Playboy, which printed 'A Breath of Lucifer' in July 1969 and 'God and the Cobbler' in February 1976 (Post45 Playboy Fiction Index).
stylistic_characteristics: Narayan told William Walsh that English 'is so transparent it can take on the tint of any country', and Walsh called his English 'limpid, simple, calm and unaffected, natural in its run and tone, and beautifully measured' (Contemporary Authors). Walsh also described the typical design of the novels as concentric circles, with the town outside, the family within and a modest, self-aware hero at the hub, and called them 'comedies of sadness'. Melvin J. Friedman placed him, with Isaac Bashevis Singer, in an oral tradition in which the spoken triumphs over the written. Gale's Contextual Encyclopedia stresses the economy of his plotting, and notes that the stories of his early collections are slight and journalistic, those of the later ones longer and more intricately built.
intellectual_concerns: Middle-class life in a small South Indian town and the meeting of tradition and modernity there; money, ambition and the vanity of human wishes (The Financial Expert); imposture and sainthood (The Guide); the national movement and Gandhi (Waiting for the Mahatma); fathers and sons and the generation gap (The Vendor of Sweets); a bully's invasion of a quiet life, told through a Hindu myth (The Man-Eater of Malgudi); love set against a woman's vocation (The Painter of Signs); renunciation and detachment (A Tiger for Malgudi); the retelling of Hindu myth and epic; and the comedy of misunderstanding between India and the West ('A Horse and Two Goats', Talkative Man).
historical_significance: Graham Greene called him 'the novelist I most admire in the English language' (Contemporary Authors), the poet Dom Moraes 'by far the best writer of English fiction that his country has ever produced' (Gale), and Shashi Tharoor wrote that in the West he was widely considered the quintessential Indian writer. Critics compare Malgudi with Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County, and Walsh wrote that 'whatever happens in India happens in Malgudi, and whatever happens in Malgudi happens everywhere'. The Guide won the first Sahitya Akademi Award for English, and in 1994 he became the second Indian writer in English, after Anand, to be made a Fellow of the Akademi. V. S. Naipaul's reading of his novels as 'religious books ... intensely Hindu', prepared for withdrawal rather than action, is a political critique that later critics, Richard Cronin among them, have examined (eNotes).
